catalog_quote: p.58: "Systematic Phonetic Tones in Ìyàyú. A careful examination of Ìyàyú dialect systematic phonetic level reveals that the dialect has high, low and mid tones. i. The high tone is realized phonetically in Ìyàyú dialect. It can be found in word initial, medial and final positions as shown in the following examples." p.59: "ii. The low tone is common and has free occurrence in the dialect. It appears in word initial, medial and final positions ... iii. The mid tone is also found in Ìyàyú dialect. There is no restriction as to where it can appear or occur. ... Functions of Tone in Ìyàyú. Tone performs both lexical and grammatical functions. Tone performs lexical functions in a language when lexical items with identical segmental phonemes are distinguished on account of tonemes." p.60: "The study also found out that Ìyàyú is a tonal language with three functional pitch levels. They are High [ ́], Mid, and Low [ ̀]. These tones are functionally load-carriers. They are used lexically and grammatically for distinguishing words which are segmentally identical."

new_statements.rule_in_words: Iyayu is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L) with lexical and grammatical (tense-marking) tone; the article gives no statement about word stress or accent anywhere (the words 'stress' and 'accent' do not occur).
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Tone: H, M, L all occur word-initially, medially and finally; tone distinguishes present/continuous vs past.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone illustrated on isolated words (SIL 1700-item wordlist elicitation from 30 speakers aged 60+) and a few sentence pairs; syllable types V and CV only, no codas or clusters.
new_statements.identity_note: The source describes the speech of Ìyàyú quarter of Ìdó-Àní (Ido-Ani) town, Ọ̀sẹ́ LGA, Ondo State — exactly Glottolog iyay1238 (alt. name Idoani). The authors call it a 'dialect' but treat it as an Edoid (North-Western Edoid) lect not mutually intelligible with the Yoruba-like speech of the other five quarters; oral tradition links the group to Sósan (Akoko South-East), matching Glottolog's 'Sosan = Iyayu' mapping for Oyebade & Agoyi 2004.
